# Sirijātaka (Ja 284)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Thief of Luck

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sirijātaka* (Ja 284) is a canonical birth story preserved in the *Abbhantaravagga* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1879; SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens around a story told by the Buddha concerning a brahmin who attempted in vain to steal the good luck (*siri*) of the wealthy householder Anāthapiṇḍika [Fenn 1994; SuttaCentral]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the king of that past lifetime was Ānanda and the royal ascetic advisor (*kulūpaka-tāpasa*) was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].

The text's principal thematic teaching centers on the doctrine of karma: good fortune and wealth are the fruition of virtuous deeds (*katapuñña*) performed in previous lives, demonstrating that merit cannot be stolen or appropriated by another [Fausböll 1879; Fenn 1994]. Miranda Shaw notes that the story focuses on the figure of Śrī Lakṣmī, affirming that wealth and blessings arise as the karmic result of past meritorious acts [Shaw]. Mavis Lillian Fenn highlights the work as a rare canonical discourse explicitly connecting accumulated merit (*puñña*) with transcendent welfare, illustrating the inviolability of personal karma [Fenn 1994]. Outside textual recitation, the story acquired iconographic importance in Southeast Asian Buddhist traditions, with scenes from the *Sirī Jātaka* depicted on temple panels in Cambodia [Harris 2005].

According to DharmaNexus, the text shares three internal reuse matches (totaling 310 characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), with its largest overlapping passage corresponding to segments §1.1–2.4 aligned with commentary segments §2630–2634 [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus records no cross-language matches above threshold [DharmaNexus], and SuttaCentral records no curated cross-language parallels, while listing four modern translations [SuttaCentral].
